title: This Portfolio Site
summary: A data-driven portfolio of more than 60 projects, built with Vite, React, and Tailwind, with every project stored as JSON and the whole site published free on GitHub Pages.
description:
This site is the portfolio you are reading. Its purpose is to show the work behind a resume. A resume has room for a line or two on each project, and this site holds the whole story behind each one, with the evidence, so a reader can go as deep as they like.

It separates what I built from what I led. Over 20 years I have both written software and managed teams, programs, and platforms, and a single list would blur the two. So the projects are split into three tabs: Developed (things I built myself), Managed (programs and platforms I led, oversaw, or advised, where my teams built the work and I owned the outcome), and Prototypes (experiments and unfinished ideas). A short Featured row leads each of the first two.

There is no back end. Every project is an entry in a JSON file, with a title, summary, description, year, tags, links, and optional screenshots and a demo. Adding a project means editing that file and pushing. A demo can be a link, an embedded page, or a React component that is loaded only when its page is opened. Screenshots open in a lightbox with zoom and captions.

Finding things is a first-class feature. Search covers titles, descriptions, tags, and a set of extra keywords, and tags filter the list. I reduced more than 200 ad hoc tags to about 55 canonical ones so filtering is useful, and kept the originals as searchable keywords and as an "Also" line on each project. The tab, search, and tags all live in the URL, so any filtered view can be bookmarked or shared.

It is built with Vite, React 19, React Router, and Tailwind CSS 4. It uses hash-based routes because GitHub Pages cannot rewrite deep links, and a small scroll manager that starts new pages at the top but restores your position when you go back, which keeps phone scrolling from fighting you. The page works in light and dark mode and on phones, and it has link-preview metadata so a shared link shows a proper card. A GitHub Actions workflow builds the site and deploys it to GitHub Pages on every push to main.

I built it with Claude Code, working in short iterations: I supplied the content and decisions, and checked the results in a real browser, including a headless browser test for the behaviors that broke along the way.

title: Tasty Tracker
summary: A trade-journaling SaaS product I founded in 2018 and still run.
description:
Tasty Tracker is a subscription trade-journaling product. I own everything: strategy, pricing, development, releases, payments, production support, and customer feedback.

The prior version grew to 2,725 members. I later rebuilt it on Laravel. The original used no framework, so moving to a standard one sped up development, made features like OAuth sign-in straightforward, helped ensure security, and gave me something new to learn. The rebuild has 151 members and is growing.

What it does: members log options and stock trades into portfolios, group them into positions, and follow them from open to close, including scaling, dividends, and reopening. The app identifies each position's strategy, calculates buying power for equity and futures, and rolls results up by security, strategy, and time, with a trade list and activity history. A signal engine compares each open position's profit against the time held and the time remaining to suggest holding, closing, or rolling, and scheduled jobs send profit-target and expiry alerts by email and in-app notification. Around the journal there is a diary, a social feed with following, blocking, direct messages, and public profiles, a blog with comments, and a dashboard of market indicators: investor and consumer sentiment, market breadth, the McClellan oscillator, credit spreads, drawdowns, days since the market's high, year highs and lows, an overnight futures chart, and an economic calendar.

The web app: Laravel 12 on PHP 8.2 with MySQL, upgraded in place from Laravel 10. Fortify handles authentication, Sanctum handles sessions and personal API tokens, and Socialite provides OAuth2 sign-in with Google, GitHub, Facebook, and Twitter. Billing uses Cashier with Stripe checkout, a customer portal, and webhooks. The REST API is versioned, built with Eloquent API resources and form requests, and documented with Swagger. Laravel Pulse, a job-run table, and a scheduled health check watch production, and an admin area can re-run background jobs and impersonate users for support. The front end is built with Vite and uses jQuery, JsRender templates, Bootstrap 5, Chart.js, Luxon, Quill for the blog editor, Cropper for profile photos, and html2canvas for sharing a position as an image. It also uses my own idle-session package to keep session timeouts in sync across tabs. Email is sent through AWS email.

Background work: a single cron entry triggers Laravel's scheduler, which keeps a prioritized queue worker running (high, medium, low), pulls market indicator data on a schedule, caches heavy calculations such as drawdowns and days since the high, refreshes market snapshots for open positions, and purges stale unverified accounts. Every job records its status so a health check can tell me when something stops running. A separate beta environment runs the same code with the data jobs switched off and a weekly wipe-and-reseed.

The Node component: a companion Node.js service streams live market data. It runs in Docker on Node 20, uses node-cron on New York time to open and close WebSocket streams around the trading day and the overnight futures session, and trades OAuth2 refresh tokens for short-lived stream tokens. It writes minute, daily, and monthly price records into the same MySQL database the web app reads from, and after the close it backfills daily and monthly candles for the S&P 500 index. It reports each run to the shared job-run table, and it forwards persistent errors to a Discord webhook with thresholds and cooldowns so a flapping error cannot flood the channel. GitHub Actions builds the image into GitHub Container Registry on every push to main, and the server pulls it with Docker Compose.

Deployment and quality: tagging a release in GitHub starts an Actions workflow that builds the front end with Vite, syncs the files to shared hosting, and then over SSH puts the site into maintenance mode, updates dependencies with Composer, runs migrations, caches configuration, routes, events, and views, regenerates the API docs, and brings the site back up. There are more than 90 database migrations and a PHPUnit suite covering authentication, the API, and the data jobs.

title: LeaseTracker
summary: A property-management SaaS with online rent payments, a tenant portal, and a native Android app.
description:
I have owned rental real estate since I was 18 and finally got tired of tracking everything manually, so I built LeaseTracker, launched in September 2026. It is a multi-tenant SaaS: each property-management company gets its own isolated workspace, and one tenant can belong to more than one company.

What it does: companies manage apartments, units, tenants, and leases, with a ledger of charges and payments per lease. Rent charges are generated automatically each month, late fees are applied on schedule, and tenants can be put on autopay. Utility bills, property taxes, and insurance policies are tracked per property, and utility bills can be charged back to tenants. It also covers maintenance records, contractors and contractor payments, document storage, unit photos, owner records with shareable owner statements, management fees, a tenant intake link for applicants, and support tickets between tenants, companies, and the platform. Analytics roll up revenue, occupancy, and balances per unit, per apartment, and across the portfolio.

Three separate logins share one codebase: company staff, tenants (a self-service portal for balance, lease, documents, and paying or reporting a payment), and a platform admin area with cross-company analytics and the ability to suspend or reactivate companies.

Payments use two independent Stripe integrations. Rent collection uses Stripe Connect Express, so each company connects its own account and tenant card or ACH payments land directly with them. Platform billing uses Laravel Cashier with a base subscription plus a graduated per-active-tenant price. Companies can also list manual channels such as Zelle, Cash App, or check, and a tenant-reported payment stays pending until a company user confirms it. Both webhooks and the billing screens degrade gracefully until keys are configured, and companies start on a 14-day trial.

The web app: Laravel 12 on PHP 8.2 with MySQL, using database-backed sessions, queues, and cache. Views are Blade with Bootstrap 5 and Bootstrap Icons, built with Vite and Sass. Chart.js draws the analytics, Tom Select powers searchable pickers, and the qrcode library generates QR codes. Sign-in supports email and password plus Google through Socialite, and users can turn on two-factor authentication with a TOTP authenticator app using Google2FA. Intervention Image resizes unit photos. Policies enforce who can touch what, and a scheduler runs the daily jobs: rent charges, rent-due emails, a payment reminder cadence, autopay charging, late fees, and suspending expired trials. Email goes out through AWS SES over SMTP, errors are forwarded to a Discord webhook through a custom log handler, and I reused my own idle-session script to log out inactive users.

The Android app: rather than maintain a second codebase, the app is a Capacitor 8 shell whose WebView loads the live site, so it shares the same Blade views, session-cookie auth, and CSRF protection as the web version. Landlords and tenants use the same app and just sign in to their own section. The native pieces are what make it more than a wrapped website: push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging (Capacitor Firebase Messaging on the device, and a custom Laravel notification channel that calls the FCM HTTP API using a Google service account), biometric sign-in with fingerprint or face unlock (Capgo native biometric plugin plus server-issued biometric tokens), native Google sign-in that hands the session back to the WebView through a one-time exchange, camera access for uploading photos and documents, an in-app browser for external links such as Stripe onboarding, and Android back-button handling and pull-to-refresh. It targets Android 7.0 and up (minSdk 24) and compiles against SDK 36 with Gradle in Android Studio. Release builds are signed Android App Bundles uploaded to Google Play with Play App Signing. I prepared the store listing assets, the privacy policy, account-deletion page, and the Data Safety disclosure.

Deployment and quality: every push to main deploys to a beta environment with its own database through GitHub Actions, and publishing a GitHub Release deploys production. The workflow builds the assets with Vite, uploads an archive over SCP to shared hosting, then over SSH runs Composer, migrations, and the cache steps. There are 57 database migrations and a PHPUnit suite of about 70 feature and unit tests that runs against in-memory SQLite, covering payments, autopay, late fees, rent generation, biometric and Google login, device tokens, account deletion, and more. Laravel Pint keeps the code style consistent.

I built it alongside a full-time job, and AI-assisted development made that practical.

title: Contractors
summary: An invite-only app for a group of friends to log contractors they've hired and review them.
description:
A small Laravel app so that I and a few friends can record which contractors we have used and what we thought of them. Each review has the price paid (optional), a rating, a written review, and photos, and members can search by service to see who has actually been used before.

Access is invite-only: any member can generate a shareable link that expires after seven days or one use, and the new person supplies their own details or signs in with Google. Google sign-in links to an existing member by email, or creates an account only when it arrives through a valid invite, and an unknown email with no invite is turned away. Contractor entries are shared and any member can edit them, while reviews are personal, so only the author can change or delete them, and one member can review the same contractor more than once. Services are a fixed set of tags rather than free text, which keeps search consistent. There is an admin role with an activity log and the ability to ban members.

It was built over a few days in September 2026 with a feature test suite covering invites, Google login, reviews and photos, tags, bans, and the activity log, and has a GitHub Actions deploy workflow.

title: PHP Rental Manager
summary: My first attempt at a site for managing my rental properties, years before LeaseTracker.
description: A simple PHP website for managing rentals, with a login, a list of apartments, a detail page for each, and a small API to read and save apartment records. I built it in May 2018 to track my own properties, and the idea eventually grew into LeaseTracker.

title: Cheesecake
summary: A transparent family-monitoring app: an Android client syncs a child's messages and calls to a private parent dashboard.
description:
Cheesecake is a parental-control tool I built for my own family. An Android app on a child's phone sends text messages, group chats, and call history to a private web dashboard that the parents read. It does not hide: it runs as a visible foreground service, and the child's phone shows what it is doing.

The Android client is a single Java app with no Gradle: a PowerShell script drives the Android SDK command-line tools (aapt2, javac, d8, zipalign, apksigner) to produce a signed APK. A foreground service watches the phone's SMS, MMS, and call-log tables with content observers, so new messages sync in near real time, with a low-frequency poll as a safety net and a heartbeat when nothing is new. That design avoids wake locks and keeps battery use low. Syncs are idempotent and keyed on the phone's own ids, so a dropped connection can safely resend a batch.

One gap showed up in real use: some RCS group conversations keep new messages only inside Google Messages' own database and never write them to the shared SMS provider. To cover that, a notification listener service captures group-chat notifications from Google Messages only, and ignores every other app and all one-to-one chats. The app asks for only the permissions it needs: no location, camera, or microphone. Contacts are looked up one number at a time to show a name and are never uploaded in bulk. The settings screen sits behind a parental password that re-locks whenever the app leaves the foreground. The app also updates itself: every sync response tells it the newest build, and it downloads the APK from the family's own server, checks the SHA-256 hash, and hands it to Android's package installer, which only accepts an update signed with the same key.

The server is Laravel 12 on PHP 8.2 with a Tailwind and Vite front end. Each phone authenticates with its own bearer token, stored only as a SHA-256 hash, and a single API endpoint validates and upserts threads, messages, and calls inside a transaction. A deactivated device just starts getting 401s, so the app goes quiet with nothing to uninstall. The parent dashboard has conversation threads, full-text search, a call log, and a device page, and installs to a phone's home screen as a progressive web app. Each device has its own retention window, and a daily scheduled job purges older messages and calls, writes a status file that shows whether it actually ran, and removes empty threads. Artisan commands add parents and devices and report device status. A public install guide walks through setup on the child's phone, and a deploy script packages the app for shared hosting.

title: Integration Engine (in progress)
summary: A new integration engine with a high-performance Rust core and a TypeScript developer experience.
description:
In October 2026 I started writing a new integration engine from scratch. The core is written in Rust for performance, and developers write their interfaces in TypeScript.

It is meant to hold the lessons from 20 years of integration work, with automatic documentation, monitoring, testing, examples, edge cases, and scalability built in from day one rather than bolted on.

title: IdleSession
summary: A zero-dependency ES module that keeps session timeouts in sync across browser tabs.
description:
IdleSession syncs idle and session timeouts across tabs using BroadcastChannel, so a user active in one tab never gets logged out by another.

It uses throttled activity listeners, heartbeats that tell a network blip apart from a real 401 or 403, and an accessible warning dialog. Tests run in GitHub Actions, and it is published to npm and served from the jsDelivr CDN.

It is the successor to my earlier jQuery idle timer plugin, rewritten with no dependencies.

title: jQuery Idle Timer
summary: A widely used jQuery plugin that fires events when a user goes idle or comes back. About 700 stars and 140 forks.
description:
jQuery Idle Timer fires a custom event when a user is idle, meaning they have stopped moving the mouse, scrolling, typing, or touching the screen, and another when they return. Idle detection like this is what logs people out of banking or healthcare sites after inactivity, or pauses work in the background.

The idea started with Nicholas Zakas's YUI idle timer and Paul Irish's jQuery port. I became the maintainer and the main contributor (54 of roughly 140 commits) and cut the 1.x releases. Features include a timer you can attach to any element rather than the whole page, configurable activity events, and optional synchronisation of activity across browser tabs through localStorage. The plugin is about 3 KB minified, ships with demos for auto-logout and multi-tab logout, and has an automated test suite.

It is now retired. The README points people to my modern replacement, IdleSession, which uses native browser APIs and has no jQuery dependency.

title: IdleTimer (ES module)
summary: A small modern rewrite of my jQuery idle timer as a plain ES module.
description: A first step away from jQuery for my idle timer: a plain JavaScript class you import as a module and configure with a timeout and onIdle and onActive callbacks, with a stop method to turn it off. It was later superseded by IdleSession, which adds multi-tab awareness, heartbeats, and session handling.

title: jQuery FormLoader
summary: A tiny jQuery library that fills a form from an object and reads it back into one.
description:
FormLoader is a small, dependency-light helper for forms with many fields. Point it at any container, not necessarily a form element, and call deserialize with an object to populate every matching input, or serialize to get all the values back as an object.

It handles text inputs, textareas, selects, checkboxes (as true or false), radio groups (by matching the option's value), and numbers (parsed to real numbers, with a data-type attribute to override how a field is read). I wrote my own serialize because jQuery's serializeArray needs a form wrapper and returns an array rather than an object.

It is a single ES module of about 100 lines. jQuery is used only to keep the code short, and I intended a sibling library without that dependency. I published it on GitHub in October 2023 and fixed its checkbox handling in November 2024.

title: supportedBrowser.js
summary: A small library that detects a visitor's browser and OS and tells you politely whether you support it.
description:
We supported a specific list of browsers and wanted to tell other visitors, gently and without blocking them, that things might not work as expected. supportedBrowser.js gathers the browser and operating system details and compares them with a list you define, returning simple booleans for your page to act on. It helps manage expectations and gives a support team the details needed to diagnose a problem.

It is split into two files: browserInfo, which only collects information, and supportedBrowser, a small function that checks it against your list. It is deliberately not a full browser-detection or feature-detection library, and the README says which of those to use instead. It has a live demo.

title: Bootstrap Typeahead Fork
summary: Extensions to Twitter Bootstrap's typeahead: AJAX sources, a minimum length, and better keyboard behavior.
description: A fork of a fork of Bootstrap 2's typeahead plugin. The earlier fork added an AJAX source, objects as the data source, an on-select callback, and up and down selection. I added a minimum length before the source is called (like jQuery UI's autocomplete), no option selected by default so tabbing leaves what you typed alone, and keyboard wrap-around that passes through a deselected state, among other changes.

title: PFP Styler
summary: A prototype that restyles a profile photo into 50+ presets while keeping the face recognizable.
description:
PFP Styler is a Python image-generation prototype from March 2026. It uses InstantID through the Replicate API to restyle a profile photo into more than 50 presets while preserving the person's face.

The presets span anime and cartoon looks, comic books, fantasy and RPG art, cyberpunk, classic painting styles, modern digital art, cinematic portraits, and cultural styles such as ukiyo-e and stained glass. Each preset is a prompt plus a negative prompt, and the interface lets you add your own negative terms to steer a result, for example to keep out hats or glasses.

In the Gradio web interface you upload a photo and pick a style. Two sliders control how closely the result follows your face and how strongly the style is applied, and you can generate up to four variations at once. Pillow center-crops the photo to a square and resizes it to 1024 pixels before it goes to the model, and the results are downloaded and saved locally. Each generation costs roughly a cent or two.

title: Trading Bender (prototype)
summary: A broker-agnostic web trading front end in Vue, modeled on Tastyworks' old web interface. Never completed.
description:
Trading Bender was meant to be a front end that sits on top of whatever brokerage you already use. The idea was that the broker supplies the back end (accounts, fees, regions) while the site supplies a focused trading interface, with a small monthly subscription and a community for sharing and following trades. I modeled the interface on Tastyworks' original web platform, which I liked better than the redesign. I started it in December 2021 and never completed it.

It is a Laravel 9 application with Inertia and Vue 3. Laravel Jetstream and Fortify supply registration, email verification, two-factor authentication, sessions, and API tokens, and visitors can also sign in with Google, Facebook, Twitter, or GitHub. Tradier was the only broker integrated, through a custom OAuth flow because Socialite does not support it. The browser talks directly to Tradier's API for accounts, positions, quotes, and symbol search, and a sandbox mode exists for practice. The main screens are a symbol lookup with live quotes (the largest piece of the app), a positions view, an order ticket, and account switching, with Bootstrap 5, Sass, and Tailwind for styling and jQuery and JsRender in places. The marketing pages, privacy policy, and terms are written, and a GitHub Actions workflow deploys to shared hosting.

It was built in a burst of about 200 commits that month, with a few follow-ups afterwards.

title: Tastyworks Mod (bookmarklet and extension)
summary: A bookmarklet and Chrome extension that decluttered the Tastyworks web trading site.
description: A tiny customization for the Tastyworks web platform: it removed the left sidebar and a few navigation links and let the trading screen use the full width. It ships as a bookmarklet you drag to your bookmarks bar and as a Chrome extension, and the entire source is a short script so anyone can edit it to remove only the pieces they want.

title: Todd's Trades (landing page)
summary: A landing page for a no-nonsense trade-alerts and training service, meant to tie into Tasty Tracker's trade history.
description:
Todd's Trades was going to be a trading alerts and training service, with a promise of trading and nothing else: no selling of information, no spam, no ads. Its trade history would be free for anyone to view, pulled from Tasty Tracker, so visitors could judge the results themselves. I only built the marketing site, and the tracking integration was never built.

The site is static HTML on a purchased Bootstrap 5 template, with jQuery, WOW.js, CountUp, and numeral.js. It does not use a JavaScript framework. It lays out four account types with their prices, minimums, and goals (a small futures account, a standard futures account, a stock and ETF options account, and an ETF dividend account) and explains the free recaps, free trade history, and intro course. A small script powers a discount estimator that totals the price of the portfolios a visitor picks, with one-way or two-way communication tiers and bundle discounts. I also wrote the terms, disclaimer, and risk-disclosure pages, and planned a course and weekly account-review videos.

title: Timesheeit (early prototype)
summary: A free time tracker I started in October 2025 and shelved after building the account foundation.
description:
Timesheeit was meant to be a free time-tracking web app. I started it over a few days in October 2025 and set it aside before building the tracking itself, and it was never deployed.

What exists is the foundation. It is built on Laravel 12 with Inertia, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, from the official React starter kit. I added sign-in through Google, GitHub, and X using Socialite, with a table that links each user to their social accounts, plus email verification through AWS email, and a two-factor authentication setup from the starter kit. A GitHub Actions workflow for deploying to a beta server was started. The time-entry features, the part that makes it a time tracker, were still on the to-do list.

title: Flask Prototype
summary: A small Python Flask web app, built to try the framework.
description: A small prototype to get hands-on with Flask: Python web routing, Jinja templates with inheritance, and SQLAlchemy with SQLite for persistence. It is deliberately simple and exists to compare the framework's feel against the others I use.

title: Biweekly Budget
summary: A native Android budgeting app on Google Play since 2016, rewritten from Java to Kotlin and Compose in 2026 without breaking existing users.
description:
Biweekly Budget is a simple envelope-style budgeting app for Android. You create budgets, record debits and credits against them, and see each budget's balance plus an overall total. It is free with a $0.99 one-time Pro upgrade that removes the free limits (10 budgets, 20 transactions per budget) and unlocks custom sort orders. I built it, shipped it, and have maintained it on Google Play since 2016.

Version 1 (2016, v0.2.3): a native Android app written in Java with SQLite storage and Google Play's in-app billing for Pro. From the first commit to a signed release took about two months. Money was stored as floating-point dollars, each budget's total was stored separately and updated by hand, and it supported Android 4.4 and up.

Version 2 (2026, v1.0.0): a ground-up rewrite in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose and Material 3, Room for the database, DataStore for settings, Play Billing 9, and the Android Gradle Plugin 9 build. It keeps the same package name, signing key, database file, launcher component and in-app product, so it ships to existing users as a normal update and their budgets and Pro purchase carry over. It requires Android 7.0 and targets Android 16.

How Pro works: Google Play is the source of truth. Each time the app comes to the foreground it asks Play which products the account owns, verifies the purchase signature against the app's licensing public key, and caches the answer for offline use. New phones, refunds and pending payments are all picked up automatically.

Testing: 74 JVM tests run with Robolectric and no device. They check the totals at every layer (repository, view model, and the real Compose screens), include a 3,000-step randomized run compared against an independent model, verify the migration against a database built exactly like the old app's, and exercise purchases, restores, refunds and pending payments against a scripted Google Play.

title: CueMaker
summary: A small utility that creates the missing .cue files RetroPie needs for PlayStation games. About 90 stars.
description:
RetroPie 4.x requires a .cue file next to each PlayStation .bin image, and the existing tools made you create them one file at a time. CueMaker scans a folder, optionally recursively, and creates a .cue file for every .bin that does not have one.

There are two versions of the same tool. A Windows Forms application written in C# needs no installation: run it and pick a folder or a single .bin. A Python script covers macOS, Linux, and the RetroPie itself, prompting for the path to scan and defaulting to RetroPie's directories. Releases are published on GitHub.

title: Clear Channel Discord Bot
summary: A small Discord bot that bulk-deletes messages from the private channel where my app's errors are posted.
description:
My Laravel apps post their error-log entries to a private Discord channel. Once I have seen and handled an error I do not want it sitting there, both for security and so an empty channel tells me I am caught up. This bot lets me type !clear, or !clear followed by a number, in that channel to wipe the messages.

It is a Node.js bot built on discord.js 14. It ignores other bots, checks that the person has the Manage Messages permission, validates the count (1 to 100, default 100), and uses Discord's bulk delete. A tiny Express server answers health checks so an uptime monitor could keep it alive on free hosting; it first ran on Replit with UptimeRobot, and now runs in Docker on an Ubuntu server with Docker Compose. A GitHub Actions workflow builds the image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry on every push.

Because a clear command is destructive, the README recommends giving the bot access to only the channels it needs.

title: Chatterbox
summary: A proof-of-concept end-to-end encrypted chat: each client held its own private key, so even the server could not read messages.
description:
Chatterbox was a proof of concept for secure chat where the server never sees a readable message.

Each client generated its own key pair in the browser and published the public key. The private key stayed in JavaScript on the client, which decrypted every received message on the fly. To send a message, the client encrypted it with the public key of the intended recipient, so the server only ever relayed ciphertext.

SignalR kept a WebSocket open to each client and pushed messages to them in real time. Getting the browser cryptography to work against a .NET back end took some tweaks and demos, which I contributed back to the Forge JavaScript crypto library.

title: Forge Open-Source Contribution
summary: A merged pull request adding the demos section to the Forge JavaScript crypto library.
description:
I contributed the demos section to Forge, a JavaScript cryptography library, and the pull request was merged. The demos included C# RSA key interoperability, showing keys moving between the JavaScript library and .NET.

The work came out of building Chatterbox, my encrypted chat proof of concept, which needed some tweaks to Forge and working examples of keys moving between a browser and a .NET back end.

title: Home Server
summary: An Ubuntu server running my Docker workloads: media, photos, music, monitoring, and bots.
description:
A home server I run on Ubuntu with Docker Compose, managed as code. Each workload is its own stack: a Jellyfin media server, Immich for photos, monitoring, and the Discord bot from my Clear Channel project, plus a backup script.

I keep a runbook and write an incident report whenever something breaks. A five-hour outage in April 2026 traced back to an Ubuntu volume sized at 100 GB of a 894 GB disk and to bind mounts that pointed at a path that never existed, so several containers' settings had been living inside the containers and getting wiped on restart. I expanded the volume and fixed the paths, and later migrated Docker from the snap package to the apt package. There is also a step-by-step guide for moving a family's photos out of Google Photos into Immich safely, with the order of steps designed so nothing is deleted until the backup is verified.

Python scripts organize movies and TV episodes, repair Jellyfin metadata and NFO files, and de-duplicate a music library. Two small tools sit alongside: a downloader that saves audio from streams with yt-dlp and ffmpeg, and a music manager built on beets that tags files using audio fingerprints, with its library kept on the NAS so it survives a PC failure. I also set up SSH access so that Claude Code can run commands on the server, with a separate non-interactive key for it.

title: Cloverleaf to Mirth Migration
summary: Evaluated the market, chose Mirth Connect, built its templates and standards, and led the move of 1,700+ live interfaces off Cloverleaf with no customer-visible downtime.
description:
The migration began in 2020. I evaluated the integration engines on the market, prototyped Mirth Connect in my spare time, and chose it as the replacement for our Cloverleaf interface engine.

From the first investigation to shutting down Cloverleaf took about three years, with gaps along the way, because the team kept doing its day jobs throughout. The time went into extensive prototyping to prove Mirth could meet our needs, contracting for its professional features, building the servers, training staff (most of whom did not know JavaScript at all), and then converting that many assets.

Before anyone migrated an interface, I created the foundation for doing it well: an interface template, and code templates that enforced our standards and kept the code clean. I then led the migration. I migrated several interfaces myself, and advised the team on best practices and on the specifics of converting from Cloverleaf.

We moved more than 1,700 live interfaces using parallel runs and output diffs, so the old and new engines could be compared message by message before each cutover. The work involved about a dozen teams and roughly 50 VPNs, and there was no customer-visible downtime.

Running both engines in parallel and diffing every output also surfaced and fixed older bugs, and the move saved about $500,000 a year.

title: My Mirth Code (public library)
summary: A public collection of Mirth Connect code templates, admin API scripts, and tools, written to be reusable.
description:
A public repository of Mirth Connect code I wrote, shared for anyone building interfaces. My approach is to put as much as possible in code templates, written in JavaScript and accepting and returning JavaScript data types. Even when the underlying Java is short, I wrap it in a JavaScript template so other developers on staff can read, use, and change it without compiling anything.

The repository holds about 150 files. The code templates are grouped by purpose: date and time functions (parsing, formatting, converting between HL7, Java, and JavaScript, diffing, and detecting the duplicated hour at daylight saving changes), arrays (including HL7 segment helpers for keeping, removing, and renumbering segments), strings, files and directories, FTP, HTTP, email, databases and SQLite, maps, E4X, and server utilities. A full PGP library encrypts to multiple keys with configurable algorithms and an integrity check, decrypts with automatic algorithm detection, and caches keys in the global channel map. There are also scripts that call Mirth's API to create, rename, move, and re-library code templates, an HTTP-listener pattern that routes a URL path to a destination of the same name to build a small REST API inside a channel, a channel-speed analytics script, and an automatic backup template that writes encrypted zip backups of the server.

title: My Cloverleaf Code (public archive)
summary: Over a hundred Tcl procedures from our Cloverleaf days, scrubbed of confidential content and shared for anyone still on the engine.
description:
We ran Cloverleaf for years and no longer do. I uploaded a large part of our old Tcl code, with everything confidential scrubbed out, in case it helps someone still running the engine. It is shared as is and is no longer updated.

The repository holds 112 Tcl procedures covering the work an interface engine does all day: building and acknowledging HL7 segments and messages, provider and NPI lookups, Epic-related routines, FTP, email, curl and JSON, GUIDs and date math, dictionary, list, and string helpers, file get and put, database save, list, and delete helpers, and daemon start, stop, and state control. A separate public repository, TCL-Tools, has general-purpose Tcl 8.5 scripts that make heavy use of dictionaries.

title: AWS Migration
summary: Led a three-person team moving 14 production servers to AWS. The ADT feed, about 1M transactions a day, could not keep up at first; after tuning and splitting the tiers, backlogs were lower than on site.
description:
In March 2026 I led the migration of 14 production servers from on-premises VMware to AWS, using NC2 and EC2. The team was me and two other developers.

We split the Mirth servers into separate application and database tiers, growing from 14 servers to 16, so each tier could be sized and scaled independently. The two developers primarily validated the systems as each wave moved. Once the tiers were split, I optimized the PostgreSQL and Mirth configurations.

The outcome came in two stages. When we first moved, the ADT feed, which carries about a million transactions a day, could not keep up. I fixed throughput by moving to a disk-optimized instance type and by the PostgreSQL and Mirth optimizations. After that work and the tier split, we had fewer backups than we ever had on site.

The move also avoided a multi-million-dollar VMware bill.

title: PostgreSQL Wraparound Recovery
summary: Rebuilt a PostgreSQL database handling 2B+ write transactions within 30 minutes of approval, then made sure it could not recur.
description:
In fall 2025 the PostgreSQL database behind our Mirth integration engine, which had handled more than 2 billion write transactions, hit transaction ID wraparound.

I argued for a clean rebuild over a slow in-place recovery, did it myself on the newest PostgreSQL version, and had it running within 30 minutes of approval. Afterward I added a weekly automated VACUUM job so it could not happen again.

title: Containerization and Cloud R&D
summary: Led the start of moving our integration platform to containers, with OpenShift manifests and research into ECS, API Gateway, and S3.
description:
In 2026 I led the start of our containerization effort. I wrote the Kubernetes manifests (YAML) for OpenShift, then planned ECS for Mirth as we moved from Red Hat servers to containers.

I also researched placing API Gateway in front of our Oracle ERP, which does not offer granular API access, and using S3 as a file-transfer option to replace much of our reliance on email, SFTP, and Windows shares, with tighter permission control and shareable links.

This work was research and development and had not moved to production.

title: Mirth Monitoring and Management Portal
summary: A web portal for interface health, debugging, reporting, and the build, debug, and deploy workflow.
description:
I built a .NET web portal that put interface health, debugging, and reporting in one place, along with the build, debug, and deploy workflow for our Mirth interfaces. It has a C# Web API back end with a web front end.

Node scripts handled operational chores like starting and stopping channels, database vacuuming, and server audits that scraped ports and IP addresses into documentation.

title: ServiceNow Process Layer and Dashboard
summary: Built our development process into ServiceNow tickets, with a self-service status dashboard that other teams adopted.
description:
ServiceNow was our system of record, but it did not reflect how my team actually delivered work. I built a .NET Core and Node application, synced with the ServiceNow API, that built our development process into the ticket itself.

Each request moved through defined phases, so everyone stayed on the same page about where work stood and what came next, and a self-service view replaced status chasing. Other teams adopted it for their own work. The API sync shipped in September 2026.

title: .NET Framework to .NET Core Port with Claude
summary: Piloted Claude Code to port .NET Framework sites to .NET Core in about a third of the usual time.
description:
In 2025-26 I piloted Claude Code on my team with a real project: porting our .NET Framework sites to .NET Core. We finished in about a third of the usual time, with tests added and every change code reviewed.

I wrote the team's AI guidelines (allowed uses, mandatory review and testing of all AI output, and no PHI in the tool) and trained staff on them.

title: PGP Library for Mirth
summary: A 13-function PGP encrypt/decrypt library built on BouncyCastle for multi-vendor file feeds.
description: A shared library for Mirth that handles PGP encryption and decryption using BouncyCastle. It has 13 functions, supports signature checks, and caches keys, so many vendors with different key setups could be handled consistently.

title: HL7 Splitter and Search Tool
summary: A .NET WinForms tool that made troubleshooting HL7 message files possible.
description: During the Cloverleaf era our backend was file-based, which made troubleshooting slow. I built a .NET WinForms tool with multithreaded parsing and filters that could split and search HL7 message files quickly.

title: SheetDelta
summary: A Python tool that shows a color-coded diff between .xlsx files, even when their columns do not match.
description: SheetDelta compares two Excel workbooks and produces a color-coded diff, handling files whose columns do not line up. I used it to sync our helpdesk queue with client ticket sheets.

title: Oracle Job Scheduler
summary: A scheduler for Oracle ERP jobs with pluggable connectors, downtime windows, dependency ordering, and a load heatmap.
description: I designed and built a job scheduler for our Oracle ERP. It has pluggable connectors, downtime windows, dependency ordering between jobs, and a heatmap of scheduled load. It saved roughly 12 hours a month of manual scheduling.

title: Oracle Assets to Git
summary: A nightly export of all Oracle custom assets into git, making them searchable and versioned.
description: A nightly job exports all of our Oracle custom assets into a git repository, making them searchable and versioned. It also automated a manual runbook.

title: Oracle ERP Integrations (program I oversaw)
summary: Took over about 1,200 Oracle ERP integration assets in June 2025, trained 9 people, and replaced 12 consultants and 2 contractors in 7 months, retiring $3M+ a year.
description:
When I took over the business team in June 2025, I took over its integrations with the Oracle ERP as well: about 1,200 integration assets in Oracle. They are built with Oracle's seeded web services, Oracle Integration Cloud (OIC), BI Publisher (BIP) reports, and HCM Extracts.

The team had not been properly trained on these tools, so I acquired the training for them, nine people in all, and carved out time for them to complete it despite their busy schedules. The training was needed to remove contractors from the work and to make sure the interfaces complied with our standards.

We prioritized the integrations that were buggy or not performant and rewrote them first. We used HCM Extracts strategically, rather than letting them be the base platform for everything, and moved more of the logic into our integration engine, where it is easier to manipulate, monitor, and fan out to other systems.

The result: in seven months we replaced 12 external consultants and 2 contractors, retiring more than $3 million a year in spend with no customer impact.

title: Oracle Admin
summary: The foundation for runbooks and asset documentation on our Oracle ERP, and the home of the external scheduler and payroll automation.
description:
Oracle Admin was the foundation that made a runbook, meaning documentation of our Oracle assets, possible. It also housed the Oracle external scheduler and the payroll automation.

The scheduler and the nightly export of Oracle assets to Git are described as their own projects.

title: OHiSee: Oracle Cloud Developer for VS Code (prototype)
summary: A VS Code extension that brings Oracle Cloud ERP development into the editor: BI Publisher, Integration Cloud, and Fast Formula, with Git as the source of truth.
description:
OHiSee is a VS Code extension I built to remove the browser from Oracle Cloud ERP development: copy-pasting SQL, uploading files by hand, and switching tabs to find out why an integration failed. It is a working prototype that I have not published to the Marketplace.

BI Publisher: pull a data model from the catalog, edit its SQL as a normal file, and push it back. A .ohisee.json file in the workspace maps each local file to its catalog path, so teammates who clone the repo are already set up, and BIP reports become files in Git with diffs, branches, and code review. Whole folders can be pulled at once, and an optional auto-sync pushes on save. After an environment refresh, a Deploy All command rebuilds every mapped data model and pushes it to the active connection, creating or updating each one. A catalog browser in the sidebar shows which reports are already local. A linter checks SQL for the things that break CSV output (unprotected free-text columns, concatenation that can embed delimiters, comma-formatted number masks, SELECT *, missing aliases, legacy outer joins, and missing effective-date filters on dated tables). A preview panel detects bind variables, prompts for values, and shows sample data as a table, and Run Report downloads the real CSV.

Oracle Integration Cloud: an instance monitor replaces the browser console for day-to-day debugging, with status filtering, 30-second auto-refresh, one-click resubmit and abort, diagnostic log download, a group-by-error view that buckets failures by message, and an inline activity stream with payloads. A sidebar lists the integration catalog by package with activate and deactivate. Integrations can be exported as IAR archives with their XSLTs extracted locally, edited, and deployed back, with the deactivate, import, and activate steps handled for me. Other tools cover a schedule manager that edits iCal recurrence rules and can run a schedule now, a trigger tester that fires a payload at an integration, an XSLT test harness, and connection templates that apply connection settings across environments.

Also included: a schema explorer for common HCM, payroll, finance, and procurement tables, Fast Formula syntax highlighting and completion with remote compile, and a connection manager for Dev, Test, and Production with passwords kept in the operating system keychain through VS Code's SecretStorage. An optional LLM setting is wired for Claude or Gemini to assist with SQL and Fast Formula, the original motivation: giving an AI assistant direct access to Oracle data and schema.

It is about 7,600 lines of TypeScript, bundled with esbuild and packaged as a .vsix for side-loading. It talks to BIP over SOAP, using the catalog and report service WSDLs, and to OIC over REST. A getting-started walkthrough guides new users.

title: IIS Manager
summary: A C# web API site for managing IIS sites and promoting them from dev to prod, with backups and required documentation.
description:
IIS Manager is a C# web API and site that lets people manage their own web sites on our IIS servers and promote them from a development server to production, instead of filing requests and waiting on an administrator.

Creating a site sets up everything it needs: the application pool, the directories, and the shares. Users push to the dev server first, then to prod. The push to production is built to be safe. It takes the application offline while files are copied, and it first zips up the existing production version as a backup so a bad release can be rolled back.

It also forces basic documentation. Every site must record a link to its repository, its owners, its customers, and a brief description, so there is always an answer to who owns a site and who depends on it.

title: On-Call Management System
summary: A system the IT department used to manage on-call.
description: As a senior developer I built the system our IT department used to manage on-call.

title: Independent Physician Office Integration
summary: Designed and maintained, then managed, the integration of 28 external EMRs across 180 physician offices and 1,411 providers: results, orders, scheduling, and discharge summaries.
description:
I designed and maintained the independent physician office integration program from 2006 to 2015, then moved into managing it. It connected 28 external EMRs across 180 offices and 1,411 providers.

While we ran Cloverleaf, I used Cloverleaf Secure Courier to securely deliver lab and radiology results to the offices. Orders flowed the other way, from the physician office back to the health system. I also sent scheduling messages (SIU) and discharge summaries, and I created the monitoring and documentation that let us support the offices.

After we moved to Mirth, I wrote a secure SFTP client to deliver files to the offices, described as its own project.

I ran the go-live with each office, some of them on site.

title: Secure SFTP Delivery Client
summary: A C# console app I wrote as sole developer, running every 5 minutes to pull pending files from a custom Mirth API and deliver them to a customer's EHR.
description:
After we moved from Cloverleaf to Mirth in 2020, physician offices still needed their files delivered securely. I wrote a secure SFTP client for that.

It is a C# console application, scheduled with Windows Task Scheduler to run every five minutes. Each run connects to a custom API I built on Mirth, downloads the files pending for that customer, and securely delivers them into the customer's EHR. It ran this way from 2020 onward.

I was the sole developer: I wrote it, patched it, and deployed it. It is part of the independent physician office integration program, which I designed and maintained and later managed.

title: Blood Bank Backup Utility
summary: A pull-based backup utility with heartbeats, replacing a push that kept failing. It runs on a dozen machines, one at each site.
description:
The blood bank system sends its backups to a server, and the original design pushed them out to a backup machine at each site. That push frequently ran into trouble: the PC was down or otherwise unreachable.

I replaced it with a utility that reverses the direction. Each client pulls the latest backup from the server instead of waiting for one to be pushed, and it checks in with a regular heartbeat. If a client misses its heartbeat, or a download is not confirmed, the system messages support. It does not depend on a particular time of day. Because the clients check frequently, a delayed backup is simply picked up as soon as it becomes available.

A web admin site lets support approve new clients, see the status of each one, and retrieve their logs. It was deployed to a dozen backup machines, one located at each site.

title: WEL: Enterprise Lookup (EMPI)
summary: An enterprise master patient index with APIs, duplicate-patient workflows, and deceased-patient checks. Epic held it up as a model of clean data. I advised from 2012 and managed it from 2020.
description:
WEL, the enterprise lookup, is an enterprise master patient index (EMPI), in use from 2012 onward. It was written when we had several sources of truth for patients. It takes patient demographics from many internal and external systems and provides a lookup and a service on top, so other systems have one place to ask who a patient is.

It has APIs that let incoming external data look up our MRN. Based on match metrics, a message is either passed along or rejected into a manual work queue, with built-in queue rejection management. I used this for the independent physician offices. It also has workflows for health information management (HIM) staff to investigate duplicate patients.

The results were notable. Epic held us up as a model of a clean system, with some of the lowest data-quality issues they had seen. Because the index brings together demographics from multiple internal and external systems, it also helped with accounts-receivable rundown. It was integrated first with the Social Security Administration and later with LexisNexis to mark patients as deceased, so we do not send mailers and other communications when a loved one has passed.

I was on the initial committee for its development, acting as an advisor. In 2020 I took over management of the product, and I and another developer helped support it and migrated it to new servers.

Onboarding new facilities onto it, which has been under my responsibility since 2015, is described in its own entry: Onboarding New Facilities to the EMPI.

title: Catch and Release
summary: My idea, built in .NET in 2025: files that need manual approval are caught in a folder, and customers review and release them through a web UI, so integration stays out of weekly payroll.
description:
Catch and Release was my idea, a .NET project built in 2025 under my responsibility. Some files, payroll in particular, need a person to approve them before they continue on their way. Instead of the integration team being involved every week, files that needed manual approval were caught in a folder, and the customer decided when to release them.

Setup is done through profiles. A profile defines the catch and release directories and which customers can access those folders.

Customers sign in to a UI where they can view, delete, release, or download the files that were caught. To let them verify the data without opening a huge file, the UI shows the head and the tail of each file, meaning its first and last lines (the header and footer records). It never tries to render a whole file that is too large, and for larger files it only offers a download.

When a file is released, Catch and Release moves it on by copying it or by FTP, depending on where the source and the destination are, and the file continues through its integration. The integration team stopped taking part in producing payroll each week and only facilitated the process.

So far the only users are the payroll team, which makes it extremely high visibility and high risk. It runs weekly, for about ten files. Because it has gone well, there are plans to roll it out to more customers.

title: Open Enrollment
summary: Ran the annual benefits open enrollment project across HR tech, benefits, HR, and integration, from the June announcement to the January 1 vendor go-live.
description:
I ran the open enrollment project every year. It is a tight annual cycle with fixed dates: plan changes are announced in June, preliminary testing happens in September, the changes go live for employees in November, and they go live with the benefit vendors on January 1.

The project spans four teams and 15 people (HR technology, benefits, HR, and integration), and runs from vendor contracts and business associate agreements through go-live. We finished early in 2025 and ahead of schedule in 2026, when we onboarded three new vendor integrations for the plan year. My part was keeping the groups in step through those milestones so the vendor connections were ready when the new plan year began.

title: Patient Portal
summary: Built a patient portal from the ground up, through regulatory approval, to 80,000+ users in its first year.
description: I built the health system's patient portal from the ground up and took it through regulatory approval. It reached more than 80,000 users in its first year, and used Twilio for messaging. Later work used FHIR against our Epic installation for the portal and other tools.

title: Virtual Waiting Room and E-Visit (WebRTC prototype)
summary: An early WebRTC prototype: patients sign in to the portal, wait in a virtual waiting room, and a provider connects for a video e-visit.
description:
I prototyped a video visit product built on WebRTC, at the point when WebRTC was only just arriving in Chrome. A patient would sign in to our portal and wait in a virtual waiting room. A provider could then see who was waiting, connect to the patient, and hold an e-visit by video in the browser, with no plug-in or separate application to install.

It was too early for the organization to take it on. The technology was new and the idea was not yet understood, so it stayed a prototype. Today the health system buys this capability from a vendor, which is what the prototype was pointing at.

The core technique is in a public sample I wrote in late 2012, an open WebRTC implementation targeting a Chrome development build. A client gives a name and starts a session, an administrator sees the waiting clients and joins one, and the browsers exchange the WebRTC offer, answer, and network candidates through SignalR WebSockets until a direct connection is made. I tested it on one machine, across a local network, and externally hosted, and documented which network setups worked and which did not. It was built with ASP.NET on IIS, jQuery, JsRender, and Bootstrap.

title: Patient iOS App
summary: A native iPhone and iPad app that I built alone and shipped to the App Store in six months.
description: I was the sole developer of the health system's iOS app, written in Objective-C for iPhone and iPad. It took six months to reach the App Store, and I set up the organization's Apple developer account along the way.

title: Prescription Refill Workflow
summary: A refill system built around a pharmacy system that could not be integrated, with admin tools, an iOS barcode scanner, and a portal page.
description:
The pharmacy system could not be integrated with, so I worked around it. I built an admin tool for pharmacy staff at every location, web services behind it, an iOS app that scans prescription barcodes, and a portal page for patients.

An Android app, written by another developer, used the same web services.

title: Surgery Tracker
summary: A display board and mobile website that let families follow a loved one's progress through surgery, anonymously and HIPAA compliant.
description:
Waiting for news during a loved one's surgery is stressful. I built a surgery tracker that showed families where their patient was in the process, on a display board in the ER and on a mobile website they could open on their own phone.

Progress was shown as a small number of simple, plain-language steps rather than clinical detail. The system was designed around patient privacy: patients were tracked anonymously and it was built to be HIPAA compliant, so a family could follow along without the board exposing who anyone was.

The surgery information came from Epic over FHIR. The board and the website read the same live status.

title: Adaptive Patient Questionnaire
summary: An adaptive medical-history questionnaire patients completed on locked-down office iPads, built on the Instant Medical History APIs.
description:
Patients completed this questionnaire on office iPads through a mobile view. It was built on the Instant Medical History vendor APIs, whose rules-based branching drilled into areas of concern with more and more questions: for example, answering that you smoke opened follow-up questions about tobacco.

I built an admin UI that staff used to pair an iPad with a specific patient. When the patient finished, their answers were submitted straight to that patient's chart, so nothing had to be re-entered.

The iPads were handed to patients locked down and fenced to the premises, so a device could not leave the building and the patient could only use the questionnaire. It was simple for patients to use, and painless for provider offices to get going.

summary: A prototype exploring Apache Kafka for event streaming.

title: AWS SQS Prototype
summary: A prototype exploring AWS SQS for asynchronous messaging.

title: RabbitMQ Prototype
summary: A prototype exploring RabbitMQ for message queuing.

title: MongoDB Prototype
summary: A prototype exploring MongoDB as a document store.

title: GraphQL Prototype
summary: A prototype exploring GraphQL APIs.

title: Ruby on Rails Prototype
summary: A prototype exploring Ruby on Rails.

title: Payroll Automation
summary: Oversaw payroll automation for 24,000+ employees ($100M+ per pay period), with gated states and validation checkpoints.
description:
I oversaw the automation of payroll for more than 24,000 employees, over $100 million in each pay period. The process moves through gated states with validation checkpoints, so each step has to be verified before payroll moves on.

I also owned the HR identity feeds that create and disable downstream accounts, and moved our banking integrations to a new bank in under a year.

Catch and Release, my idea, lets customers approve the files that need a person to review them, so the integration team no longer takes part in weekly payroll production. The automation lived in Oracle Admin, alongside the external scheduler.

title: Onboarding New Facilities to the EMPI
summary: About one major facility onboarding a quarter, the largest bringing in 140,000 to 185,000 patients each. WEL analyzes overlap and tells new patients from duplicates, and my team's automation loads them into Epic gradually.
description:
Whenever a new facility joined the health system, we used WEL, our enterprise lookup (EMPI), to bring its patients in. This process has been under my responsibility since 2015, and we did about one major onboarding a quarter.

It starts with analysis. WEL compares the facility's patient population with ours and shows how much they overlap, which gives the business what it needs to make decisions about the new facility.

Next, for the patients who overlap, WEL gathers the additional demographic information and correctly identifies what is new and what is a duplicate. The patients who are new are imported into Epic, and their MRNs are created.

Populations can be massive: our five largest onboardings each brought in between 140,000 and 185,000 patients. They are loaded slowly, on purpose, so the load does not negatively affect the system. My team built the automation for this, so nobody has to manually drop files. We monitored progress and errors to make sure everything ran smoothly, and otherwise the process needed minimal oversight.

WEL itself, the enterprise lookup behind all of this, is described in its own entry: WEL: Enterprise Lookup (EMPI).

title: Pure OHS to Enterprise Health Data Conversion
summary: In 2025, joined late and converted about 1 TB for 24,000 employees from Pure OHS to Enterprise Health in about 15 days, meeting a deadline others feared they'd miss. Moving the transfers to my dev VM made it possible.
description:
In 2025 I was the developer for converting all of the employee data from Pure OHS into Enterprise Health, covering our 24,000 employees. It was not my project to own. I came in late, when the people involved had started scrambling because they were worried they would not hit their deadline. The data was about a terabyte, which is not crazy, but it was large enough that they could not get it done: they were having trouble transmitting it and formatting the load for the new system. I took it on and saw it through.

The first problem was throughput. The sender was uploading about 100 GB a day, but through our servers we could pull only about 10 GB a day, so we could not keep up and the project would have run past its deadline. I wrote a script that used multiple connections, which helped a little, but 10 GB a day was the most I could reach.

The second problem was reliability. The files were large zip archives, and I was seeing a lot of failed transfers. Their SFTP server did not allow resuming, so every failure meant starting that file again.

Routing the work through my developer VM fixed both, which I believe was because it used a different internet connection than our production servers. From my machine, each day's 100 GB took about four hours end to end: downloading it, validating it, producing the reports, backing it up, and uploading it to the new server. That was ten times what we could manage through our servers.

Then came the data itself. I formatted the data for the load and created summary reports. I validated what we received against what they said they were sending us, to make sure it had transferred correctly with no corruption. I then compared that against what had actually been loaded into the new system, which showed exactly what needed to be resent.

It took about 15 days, a push to meet their deadline, and I got it done. It was a one-time effort, part automation and part manual work. It is a good example of how I work: I can take on any task that is asked of me and see it through to completion, even when I am not the owner.
keywords: 100 GB a day vs 10 GB a day
